I now have complete findings. ## Findings: WAF per-request detail for `e2-injection-browser-ua` (CloudFront EEXAMPLE000001, acct 012345678901_1, 2026-10-10 ~19:09–19:19 UTC) ### Method note (efficiency) The recommended "create a new table" recipe was blocked — the agent role lacks `glue:CreateTable` (confirmed `AccessDeniedException`). Instead I used the **existing `default.waf_logs` Glue table, which already has partition projection enabled** (`projection.log_time.format = yyyy/MM/dd/HH/mm`, 5-min interval). Filtering on `log_time BETWEEN '2026/10/10/19/05' AND '2026/10/10/19/15'` scanned only **~3.5 MB** — no full-bucket enumeration, no stall. (The previously-stalling table was a different, non-projected one.) ### 1. The actual injection payloads — and WHERE they are **The carrier field is the URI query string (`httpRequest.args`), NOT the User-Agent.** The User-Agent on every single request (blocked and allowed) is an identical, perfectly benign Safari string: `Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 14_6) AppleWebKit/605.1.15 (KHTML, like Gecko) Version/18.0 Safari/605.1.15` A targeted signature scan of the User-Agent header (SQLi/XSS/traversal/jndi/etc.) over the whole incident window returned **zero matches**. The incident title "browser-ua" appears to be a **mislabel** — the injection is in the query string of `/catalog`. Representative payloads (URL-decoded), by matched rule group: | Rule group | URI | Query-string payload (decoded) | Attack type | |---|---|---|---| | SQLiRuleSet | `/catalog` | `id=1 UNION SELECT username,password FROM users--` | SQLi | | SQLiRuleSet | `/catalog` | `id=1' OR '1'='1` | SQLi | | CommonRuleSet | `/catalog` | `search=` | XSS | | CommonRuleSet | `/catalog` | `search=">` | XSS | | CommonRuleSet | `/catalog` | `search=javascript:alert(1)` | XSS | | CommonRuleSet | `/catalog` | `file=../../../../etc/passwd` | Path traversal / LFI | | CommonRuleSet | `/catalog` | `file=....//....//etc/shadow` | Path traversal / LFI | | CommonRuleSet | `/catalog` | `file=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` | SSRF (IMDS) | | KnownBadInputsRuleSet | `/home` | (no args; matched on request shape/headers) | Known-bad input | ### 2. Carrier confirmation Confirmed: the **URIs/paths themselves are benign** e-commerce routes (`/catalog`, `/home`, `/cart`); the malicious content lives entirely in the **query string args**. The User-Agent is clean. So: injection vector = **query parameters (`id=`, `search=`, `file=`) on `/catalog`**. ### 3. Per-request action breakdown (same single source) - **Source:** one IP, `198.51.100.40` (country **US**) — the only attacking client. - **BLOCK — CommonRuleSet: 105** (XSS, traversal, SSRF) · first 19:09:34 → last 19:19:01 - **BLOCK — SQLiRuleSet: 75** · first 19:09:29 → last 19:18:52 - **BLOCK — KnownBadInputsRuleSet: ~15** (on `/home`) - **ALLOW (Default_Action): 15** · first 19:09:40 → last 19:19:00 - Overall incident span: **19:09:29 – 19:19:01 UTC**. Priority-1 rate-based rule was in COUNT mode (did not block), consistent with the metrics brief. ### 4. CRITICAL — Did injection requests pass through to EKS origin? **YES.** **15 malicious requests were ALLOWED (action=ALLOW, Default_Action) and forwarded to the origin.** All 15 carried the **same LFI/SSRF payload that the managed rules did NOT catch**: `GET /catalog?file=/proc/self/environ` (decoded from `file=%2Fproc%2Fself%2Fenviron`) - Fired like clockwork every ~40 seconds, 19:09:40 → 19:19:00 UTC, from `198.51.100.40`, with the same benign Safari UA. - This is a sensitive-file-read / local-file-inclusion probe. Unlike `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/shadow` (which CommonRuleSet BLOCKED), the `/proc/self/environ` variant evaded all managed rules and reached the EKS backend. Example allowed rows: ``` 19:09:40 GET /catalog file=/proc/self/environ action=ALLOW 19:10:20 GET /catalog file=/proc/self/environ action=ALLOW ... 19:19:00 GET /catalog file=/proc/self/environ action=ALLOW (15 total) ``` **Bottom line:** This is a single-source (198.51.100.40, US) multi-vector injection scan against `/catalog` query parameters. WAF blocked ~195 SQLi/XSS/traversal attempts but **leaked 15 `file=/proc/self/environ` LFI probes to the EKS origin** — a genuine WAF coverage gap worth a rule tune (and an origin-side check for whether those 15 requests succeeded). ## Results
Confirmed. There is no FluentBit/firelens application log group, no ui-specific group, and only the EKS control-plane group exists. All avenues to see the ui application's actual HTTP responses are exhausted.

## Findings

**Investigative question — Did the 15 `/catalog?file=/proc/self/environ` LFI requests reach and succeed at the EKS origin (sensitive data returned) or were they rejected?**

**Verdict: UNDETERMINED (investigation gap).** No origin-side log data is available for the incident window. I could neither confirm nor rule out that the LFI succeeded. Based on available evidence I cannot assert sensitive data was exposed, but I also cannot clear it — this gap should be escalated.

### What I established
1. **Cluster identified.** Account 012345678901_1 / us-west-2 has exactly one EKS cluster: **`example-shop`** (ACTIVE, v1.34). It is the cluster backing the CloudFront origin NLB `k8s-ui-ui-0000000001` (AWS Load Balancer Controller-provisioned Service of type LoadBalancer for namespace `ui`, service `ui`).

### Access/data gaps (ranked by impact on the question)

**(a) Could not determine LFI success/failure — root blocker.**
- **kubectl is blocked.** `example-shop` uses `accessConfig.authenticationMode = CONFIG_MAP`. Every kubectl call (get svc/pods/deployments in ns `ui`) failed persistently with `error: You must be logged in to the server (the server has asked for the client to provide credentials)`. My principal is not mapped in the cluster's `aws-auth` ConfigMap, so I cannot list ui pods or read their stdout/access logs. This is the primary reason the question is unanswerable from my position.

**(b) Exact HTTP status codes for the 15 requests — NOT RECOVERABLE from available sources.**
- EKS cluster logging enables only `api`, `audit`, `authenticator` (control-plane). These do **not** record the ui application's data-plane HTTP paths, query strings (`file=/proc/self/environ`), source IP / X-Forwarded-For, response status, or body size.
- No **Container Insights** EKS log groups exist (`/aws/containerinsights/*` — none).
- No **FluentBit/FireLens/ui-specific** CloudWatch log group exists (searched `ui`, `fluent`, `fallback` — none). The ui pods' container logs are not being shipped to CloudWatch.

**(c) Evidence of credential/environ exposure — NONE FOUND, but absence is due to no data, not confirmed-clean.**
- `/aws/application-signals/data`: 0 records in the window (only a `default` stream).
- `aws/spans` (Application Signals traces): 0 records in the window; its only stream last received an event at ~2026-08-09 (epoch 1786320330389), two months before the 2026-10-10 incident. Searches for `catalog`, `environ`, `proc` returned 0 records scanned. The ui service has no usable APM/trace telemetry for the attack window.

**(d) App errors/anomalies correlated with the requests — cannot assess.** No application or access logs are reachable for the window, so no error/404/200 correlation can be made.

### Recommendation / escalation
To answer whether the LFI succeeded, one of the following is required (all outside my current access):
- aws-auth ConfigMap access (or a mapped IAM principal) to run kubectl and read ui pod logs for 2026-10-10 19:09–19:20 UTC; or
- Enabling/retrieving the NLB target application's access logs; or
- Any ui pod log shipping (FluentBit → CloudWatch) that covers the window.

Given the ui app's own stdout is the only place the HTTP 200/4xx status and any returned `/proc/self/environ` body would appear, and that source is currently unreachable, **the real impact (sensitive-data exposure vs harmless probe) remains an open gap requiring escalation to a principal with EKS data-plane / kubectl access on cluster `example-shop`.**

Also address the secondary finding: the Priority-1 rate-based rule RateBasedRule-IP-300 is in COUNT (observe-only) mode and provides no volumetric protection — evaluate changing Action Count→Block (limit 300/IP/300s). Close the observability blind spot that made the origin impact of this bypass unverifiable, so any future WAF bypass is both detectable and confirmable.**\n\nOrigin impact could not be confirmed or ruled out because there was no telemetry for the window. Enable, ideally in IaC: (1) CloudFront standard access logging on EEXAMPLE000001 to S3 (currently DISABLED — verified Logging.Enabled=false), or real-time logs to Kinesis if near-real-time visibility is needed; (2) ui-pod application log shipping on EKS example-shop (us-west-2), e.g. a FluentBit/FireLens DaemonSet to CloudWatch Logs, and/or NLB access/target logging + Container Insights. the attacker's traffic from 198.51.100.40, **15 requests were ALLOWed through to the EKS origin** between 19:09:40 and 19:19:00 UTC — every one a local-file-inclusion probe: `GET # Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### Coordinated multi-vector injection probe from 198.51.100.40, 19:09–19:19 UTC
**Description:** A single source IP 198.51.100.40 (US), spoofing a normal Safari User-Agent, ran a ~10-minute automated web-attack probe (19:09:29–19:19:01 UTC) against distribution d111111abcdef8.cloudfront.net on paths /catalog, /cart, /home. Payloads (SQLi, XSS, path-traversal, SSRF) were carried in the URI query string / POST body — NOT the User-Agent. WAF blocked ~180 of them (CommonRuleSet 105, SQLi 75) returning 403 (surfacing as the CloudFront 4xx band), while 15 LFI requests (file=/proc/self/environ) were allowed through to the EKS origin.
**Time:** 2026-10-10T19:09:29Z - 2026-10-10T19:19:01Z

## Findings

### Cause: WAF blocked ~180 SQLi/XSS/traversal/SSRF injection requests (403), 19:09–19:19 UTC
**Description:** The managed rule groups on Web ACL CreatedByCloudFront-a1b2c3d4 blocked the bulk of a multi-vector injection probe from 198.51.100.40: AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet (105 — XSS, path traversal, SSRF/IMDS) and AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet (75 — query-arg + body SQLi), returning 403 to the client. These 403s are what surfaced as the CloudFront 4xx band (~0.7–1.3%) over the same window; 5xx stayed 0 and request volume was unchanged, so there was no availability impact. The injection payloads rode in the URI query string on /catalog (and SQLi body on POST /cart), not the User-Agent.
**Cascades to:** symptom-injection-probe

### Cause: 15 LFI requests (file=/proc/self/environ) bypassed WAF and reached the EKS origin
**Description:** Of the attacker's traffic from 198.51.100.40, **15 requests were ALLOWed through to the EKS origin** between 19:09:40 and 19:19:00 UTC — every one a local-file-inclusion probe: `GET /catalog?file=/proc/self/environ` (URL-decoded). No managed rule (CommonRuleSet/SQLi/KnownBadInputs) matched this specific pattern, so WAF passed it with Default_Action=ALLOW. `/proc/self/environ` is a classic LFI target used to leak a process's environment variables (which often hold secrets/credentials). The WAF blocked the louder SQLi/XSS/obvious-traversal variants (../../etc/passwd, etc.) but this `/proc/self/environ` LFI variant evaded all managed signatures. This is a confirmed WAF coverage gap with payloads that actually reached the application. Impact to the origin is not directly observable here (CloudFront access logging disabled, 5xx stayed 0), so whether the origin returned environment contents is unconfirmed and warrants origin-side review.
**Cascades to:** symptom-injection-probe

#### Gaps
- **Origin-side outcome of the 15 leaked LFI requests cannot be determined — no telemetry captured it:** The 15 ALLOWed `GET /catalog?file=/proc/self/environ` LFI requests reached the EKS UI origin (cluster example-shop, us-west-2), but **whether they succeeded / disclosed data cannot be determined from available telemetry**. Every request-level source was unavailable for the window: CloudFront standard & realtime access logging are disabled; the EKS cluster uses CONFIG_MAP auth so kubectl is blocked (caller not in aws-auth); EKS control-plane logs cover only api/audit/authenticator (not UI app HTTP paths/bodies); no Container Insights log groups exist; and Application Signals / `aws/spans` has no data in the window (last event ~2026-08-09, ~2 months pre-incident). 5xx stayed 0 (origin did not error), but that does not confirm whether `/proc/self/environ` contents were returned. **To close this, enable origin-side request logging (EKS app/access logs or CloudFront access logging) and review the example-shop UI app for how it handles the `file=` parameter.** Note: there is an RDS cluster example-shop-catalog behind /catalog with audit/error logs — a candidate source for assessing any SQLi data impact, though the SQLi attempts were WAF-blocked.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Harden CloudFront WAF Web ACL CreatedByCloudFront-a1b2c3d4: add two Block rules — (1) block the known malicious source 198.51.100.40, and (2) a custom query-string rule for /proc/self/environ-style sensitive-file-read/LFI that bypassed all managed rule groups. Separately, enable CloudFront access logging on EEXAMPLE000001 and ui-pod log shipping on EKS example-shop so any future bypass is detectable and its impact verifiable.

## Reasoning
The managed rule groups blocked ~195 SQLi/XSS/SSRF/classic-traversal attempts (403s), but 15 LFI probes GET /catalog?file=/proc/self/environ matched no rule and — now CONFIRMED — were forwarded to the EKS origin (example-shop, ns ui, us-west-2). Whether they returned sensitive /proc/self/environ contents (env vars / AWS_ credentials) could NOT be confirmed or ruled out: no origin telemetry for the window (kubectl blocked, no Container Insights/FireLens, no traces, CloudFront logging disabled). Because origin compromise cannot be excluded, closing the WAF gap and blocking the source IP are time-sensitive. The two rules append below the six existing rules (nothing weakened) and are fully reversible. WAF logging to S3 aws-waf-logs-012345678901_1 is already working and should be retained.

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Codify the WAF hardening in the IaC that manages Web ACL CreatedByCloudFront-a1b2c3d4 so the manual change is durable across deployments.
**Description:** The manually-added Block rules (incident IPSet reference + sensitive-file-read query-string rule) will be overwritten on the next deploy from source. Add equivalent definitions to that source. Also address the secondary finding: the Priority-1 rate-based rule RateBasedRule-IP-300 is in COUNT (observe-only) mode and provides no volumetric protection — evaluate changing Action Count→Block (limit 300/IP/300s). This carries availability risk; review counted volume in CloudWatch first and switch to Block only if the limit will not affect legitimate clients.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- IaC for CreatedByCloudFront-a1b2c3d4 includes a Block rule referencing an IPSet of known malicious sources (seeded with 198.51.100.40/32).
- IaC includes a Block rule matching sensitive-file-read/path-traversal query-string patterns (at least /proc/self/environ and related /proc, /sys pseudo-paths) with URL_DECODE and LOWERCASE transforms.
- All six existing managed rule groups remain present and unchanged.
- A deliberate COUNT-vs-BLOCK decision on RateBasedRule-IP-300 is recorded (based on reviewed CloudWatch counts) and reflected in IaC if changed.

#### 2. Close the observability blind spot that made the origin impact of this bypass unverifiable, so any future WAF bypass is both detectable and confirmable.
**Description:** Origin impact could not be confirmed or ruled out because there was no telemetry for the window. Enable, ideally in IaC: (1) CloudFront standard access logging on EEXAMPLE000001 to S3 (currently DISABLED — verified Logging.Enabled=false), or real-time logs to Kinesis if near-real-time visibility is needed; (2) ui-pod application log shipping on EKS example-shop (us-west-2), e.g. a FluentBit/FireLens DaemonSet to CloudWatch Logs, and/or NLB access/target logging + Container Insights.
